screens.title: Understanding Core Azure Storage Services for Data
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will get a practical view of the main Azure storage services and how to pick between them. We will treat storage as a set of trade-offs: object versus file versus block disk, hot versus cold access, and local versus geo redundancy. You will learn clear rules of thumb for common scenarios, such as storing data lakes, serving virtual machines, sharing files across servers, and keeping messages for asynchronous apps. I will show concrete examples, for instance when a log stream should be an append blob and when a VM operating system disk should be an Azure Disk. We will also examine access tiers and redundancy settings and why selecting the wrong one can either inflate costs or expose you to unacceptable downtime. By the end you will be able to map a workload’s access pattern, durability needs, and latency tolerance to a storage design that balances cost and reliability. Think about a scenario you manage now and imagine where those files, logs, or VM disks would live in Azure — that mental mapping will guide the lessons ahead.

screens.narratorSegment: These objectives focus your attention on the decisions a data engineer must make about storage. First, you will accurately differentiate the primary Azure storage services—Blob, Files, Disks, Table, and Queue—so you can pick the right technology for a workload. Second, you will identify concrete use cases for each service by matching data characteristics and access patterns to service capabilities. Third, you will explain the three core blob types—Block, Page, and Append—understand when to use each, and see examples such as data lakes, VHDs, and logging. Fourth, you will describe access tiers and how Hot, Cool, and Archive affect costs and retrieval latency, and make a sensible tier recommendation for backups versus active analytics. Each objective connects a concept to a clear design decision. Practice mapping a workload to these objectives and you will be able to justify storage choices to stakeholders.

screens.title: Azure Storage Services Overview
screens.narratorSegment: Azure provides a set of storage primitives, each designed for a particular data shape and access pattern. Object storage, represented by Azure Blob Storage, holds unstructured data such as images, videos, data lake files, and backups. It is highly scalable and is the default choice when you need to store large blobs of data without a fixed schema. Azure Files is managed file storage that exposes SMB shares and is ideal when you have lift-and-shift applications that expect a network file system. Azure Disks are block-level persistent volumes attached to virtual machines; they behave like traditional hard drives and are optimized for low-latency VM workloads. For key-value or semi-structured data, Azure Table Storage offers a simple, scalable NoSQL store with high throughput. Azure Queue Storage provides simple message queuing for decoupling application components and supporting asynchronous work. A common misconception is thinking one storage type fits all workloads; in practice you must match data shape and access patterns to the most fitting primitive. For example, storing VM disks in Blob Storage is inappropriate because you need low-latency block operations and persistent attachments provided by Disks. Consider a media server storing video files: Blob Storage is the right choice. For a shared configuration folder used by multiple VMs, Azure Files is the correct fit. Always ask: what is the data shape, how often is it accessed, and what latency and transactional model does the application require?

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Azure Storage Services Overview
What each service is for
Azure Blob Storage — Object
Massive, scalable storage for unstructured files and data lakes.
Azure Files — Shared file system
SMB-accessible managed file shares for lift-and-shift apps.
Azure Disks — VM block storage
Persistent low-latency disks attached to virtual machines.
Azure Table Storage — NoSQL
Key-value store for semi-structured data with high throughput.
Azure Queue Storage — Messaging
Simple queueing for asynchronous and decoupled processing.
Key Takeaway

Different data shapes and access needs determine the storage primitive you should use. Match them to reduce cost and complexity.

Example
A media archive of video files is best stored as block blobs; a VM operating system disk belongs on an Azure Disk.
Common misconceptions
  • Assuming Blob Storage can replace disks for VM boot volumes. It cannot: disks provide block attach semantics and low-latency IOPS.
  • Believing Files always offers better performance for shared data. Files provides SMB semantics but performance depends on chosen tier and protocol.
  • Thinking Table Storage is a full document database. It is a simple key-value store suited to wide, schemaless records with high throughput needs.
Try this
For a workload you manage, write down the data shape, access frequency, and latency needs. Then map each item to one storage primitive and justify the choice.

screens.title: Azure Blob Storage Deep Dive
screens.narratorSegment: Blob storage is the backbone for storing large amounts of unstructured data in Azure and a default choice when you need scalability and cost-efficiency. As a data engineer you will use blobs to house data lakes, raw ingestion layers, media, backups, and large export files. The key reasons are its flat namespace with containers, efficient large-object uploads, and the ability to set access tiers to manage cost according to frequency of access. A useful analogy is to think of Blob Storage as a warehouse: containers are aisles, blobs are crates. Block blobs are the standard crates used for most files; they let you upload parts in parallel for efficiency. Page blobs are like a set of indexed drawers where you can perform random reads and writes at the page granularity, and are used for virtual hard drives. Append blobs are a chronological log: each write appends to the end efficiently, making them ideal for telemetry or audit trails. A common mistake is storing append-heavy logs as block blobs and rewriting files; this causes extra operations and cost. For a concrete example, imagine ingesting sensor telemetry: use append blobs or write to a queue and flush to block blobs depending on downstream processing. The takeaway is to treat blob types as tools—choose the one that matches your read/write pattern to reduce latency and control cost.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Azure Blob Storage Deep Dive
Blob types and when to use them
Block blob
Optimized for large file uploads and general object storage; most data lakes and media use block blobs.
Page blob
Supports random read/write operations at page granularity; used for VHDs and persistent VM disks.
Append blob
Optimized for append operations; ideal for logs and audit trails where data is continually appended.
Example scenario
A streaming telemetry application appends events continuously; append blobs let you add entries without rewriting entire files, reducing write operations and cost.
Operational notes
  • Block blobs support parallel block uploads for high throughput and efficient large-file transfer.
  • Page blobs allow random writes but are billed differently than block blobs and are optimized for VM scenarios.
  • Append blobs are append-only; they are not designed for arbitrary overwrites.
Key Takeaway

Choose a blob type that matches your read/write characteristics. Matching reduces operations, cost, and latency.

screens.title: Block Blob Upload and Use Patterns
screens.narratorSegment: Block blobs are designed for efficient large-file uploads. The common pattern is to split a large file into blocks, upload each block in parallel, and then commit the block list to assemble the final blob. This approach reduces end-to-end latency and improves throughput when you have large objects such as parquet files or media. A concrete example: a 10 gigabyte export can be sliced into 64 megabyte blocks, each uploaded concurrently. After all blocks are uploaded, a commit operation composes the blob from the ordered block list. A frequent misconception is believing you must upload the whole file in one request; parallel block uploads avoid that and support resumable transfers if a single block fails. For data lakes, store immutable snapshots of raw ingested data as block blobs and apply downstream processing to create optimized formats. Also consider lifecycle management: set rules that transition older blobs from Hot to Cool or Archive to reduce long-term cost. Remember to align block size, concurrency, and retry logic to the storage account’s performance characteristics and your network bandwidth. The core insight is that block blobs make large-file handling efficient and reliable when you use a block-oriented upload pattern.

keyIdea.text: Split large files into blocks, upload in parallel, then commit an ordered block list to assemble the final blob; this enables resumable and high-throughput transfers.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Block Blob Upload and Use Patterns
Upload steps
1
Split the file into blocks sized for your throughput and network stability.
2
Upload blocks in parallel and verify checksums where possible to allow retries per block.
3
Commit the ordered block list to stitch the final blob together.
Example
A 10 GB export split into 64 MB blocks gives many parallel uploads and faster completion than a single large upload.
Why this matters for data lakes
Data lakes ingest large, immutable files. Using block blob patterns reduces upload time, allows resumable transfers, and keeps the raw layer stable for downstream transformation. Pair this with lifecycle rules to move older files to lower-cost tiers.
Common mistake
Uploading entire large files in a single request can lead to failures and slow retries. Use block uploads instead.
Key Takeaway

Split and parallelize large uploads; this improves throughput and resilience and is the recommended pattern for block blobs.

screens.title: Page and Append Blobs: When to Use Each
screens.narratorSegment: Page blobs and append blobs solve two distinct problems. Page blobs are optimized for random read and write operations at the page granularity and are primarily used for virtual hard disks attached to VMs. If your workload needs low-latency random writes—like updating sectors on a virtual disk—page blobs provide the required performance and semantics. Append blobs, by contrast, are optimized for adding data to the end of a blob. They are append-only, making them efficient for logging, telemetry, and audit trails where new records are regularly appended and older records are not modified. An important contrast: page blobs allow arbitrary updates but are billed and optimized differently; append blobs do not support arbitrary in-place changes. A practical example: when running a fleet of servers that emit log events, using append blobs for each server log allows you to continuously append without rewriting files. If you instead used block blobs and rewrote each file with new entries, you would incur extra operations and cost. Misunderstandings often arise when teams choose blob types by habit; the right selection reduces operational overhead and improves performance. Ask whether your workload needs random writes, or predominantly appends, and choose page or append accordingly.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Page and Append Blobs
Page blob (random write)
Designed for random read/write at page granularity. Primary use: VHDs for virtual machines where sectors are updated in place.
Example
A VM OS disk requires low-latency random writes; a page blob stores the VHD with appropriate semantics.
Append blob (append-only)
Optimized for append operations; ideal for logs, audit trails, and sequential event streams where data is only added to the end.
Example
Collecting server logs in an append blob avoids the cost and complexity of rewriting files for each new entry.
Common mistake
Using block blobs and rewriting files for append workloads increases operations and cost. Choose append blobs for logging patterns.
Key Takeaway

Match the blob type to the write pattern: random writes need page blobs; append-only streams need append blobs.

screens.title: Access Tiers: Hot, Cool, Archive
screens.narratorSegment: Azure Blob Storage supports access tiers that let you trade storage cost against access cost and latency. The Hot tier is for frequently accessed data and offers the lowest read costs but slightly higher storage costs. Use Hot for data actively processed in analytics pipelines. The Cool tier is for data accessed less frequently and stored for at least thirty days; it provides lower storage costs but higher access and retrieval costs, making it suitable for short-term backups or snapshots. The Archive tier targets long-term retention where retrieval latency of hours is acceptable; it has the lowest storage cost but the highest retrieval and rehydration cost and latency. A practical example: seven-year compliance logs with infrequent retrieval are ideal for Archive; immediate analytics data belongs in Hot. A common misconception is keeping all data in Hot to avoid retrieval complexity; that increases long-term storage costs unnecessarily. Lifecycle management rules can automate tier transitions. For instance, move raw ingestion files from Hot to Cool after thirty days and then to Archive after a year. Always account for potential retrieval costs and rehydration time when you place critical data in Archive.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Access Tiers: Hot, Cool, Archive
Hot
Optimized for frequent access. Lowest access cost, higher storage price. Use for active analytics and frequently read content.
Cool
For infrequently accessed data stored for at least 30 days. Lower storage cost, higher access cost. Good for short-term backups.
Archive
Lowest storage cost, highest retrieval cost and latency. Use for long-term archives where retrieval in hours is acceptable.
Lifecycle example
Automate transitions: Hot → Cool after 30 days → Archive after one year for long-term cost savings while keeping recent data hot.
Key Takeaway

Tiers let you align storage cost to access patterns. Use lifecycle rules to automate transitions and avoid manual rehydration surprises.

screens.title: Azure Storage Accounts and Performance Options
screens.narratorSegment: Azure storage is organized under a storage account, which provides the namespace and billing scope for blobs, files, queues, and tables. The General-purpose v2 account is the recommended, flexible choice because it supports all data services and access tiers. Premium block blob accounts are available when workloads need consistently low latency and high throughput for block blobs; these accounts provide storage media and performance characteristics optimized for those scenarios. When choosing an account type consider workload performance needs, latency bounds, and cost. For many analytics workloads, GPv2 with Standard performance is sufficient and more cost-effective. But when you run latency-sensitive real-time workloads or require consistently high IOPS for block blobs, a Premium block blob account may be necessary. A common error is selecting Premium for convenience without measuring whether the workload truly needs the performance profile; this increases cost unnecessarily. Another consideration is regional availability of account types and the interaction with redundancy options. For a concrete practice, audit your read/write latency, throughput, and IOPS requirements before selecting an account type to ensure you match performance and cost to business needs.

keyIdea.title: Account selection

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Storage Accounts & Performance
Account types
General-purpose v2 (GPv2) supports blobs, files, queues, tables and access tiers and is the typical default. Premium block blob accounts are specialized for high-performance block blob workloads.
Example decision
If you run interactive workloads that require sub-10 millisecond reads at scale from block blobs, evaluate Premium block blob accounts. Otherwise, GPv2 is usually sufficient.
Operational checklist
  • Measure IOPS and throughput before choosing Premium.
  • Check regional availability and cost implications for the chosen account type.
  • Consider lifecycle, tiering, and redundancy in the account configuration.
Key Takeaway

Choose the account to match performance needs. Default to GPv2 for flexibility; reserve Premium for measured high-performance needs.

screens.title: Redundancy Options Overview
screens.narratorSegment: Redundancy settings determine where and how Azure stores copies of your data and are central to durability and availability planning. Locally-redundant storage, LRS, replicates data three times within a single data center; it protects against drive or rack failures but not against a full data center outage. Zone-redundant storage, ZRS, replicates synchronously across availability zones within a region to protect against data center failures while keeping data in the primary region. Geo-redundant storage, GRS, replicates data asynchronously to a secondary region in addition to local replication; this protects against regional disasters. Read-access GRS, RA-GRS, provides read access to the secondary region, which can be useful for disaster recovery drills or read-heavy scenarios during failover. Geo-zone-redundant storage, GZRS, combines zone redundancy in the primary region with asynchronous replication to a secondary region for the highest durability and availability. RA-GZRS adds read-access to that secondary region. The common trade-off is cost versus resilience: higher redundancy levels cost more but provide stronger protection. screens.title: Choosing Redundancy: A Decision Checklist
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing redundancy is a risk and cost decision. Start by clarifying business requirements: what is your Recovery Point Objective and Recovery Time Objective? If your RPO is very small and you require fast failover across zones, ZRS or GZRS may be appropriate. If you need protection from a whole-region outage and can tolerate asynchronous replication lag, GRS or GZRS becomes relevant. Ask whether read-access to a secondary region is helpful for your operations; RA-GRS and RA-GZRS enable reads from the secondary copy which can be useful during outages or for geo-load distribution. Next, review budget constraints: higher redundancy increases replication costs. Run a simple decision checklist: identify critical datasets, ask if zone-level protection is needed, ask if region-level protection is required, and map each dataset to LRS, ZRS, GRS or GZRS accordingly. A common pitfall is assigning the same high redundancy to all storage by default instead of prioritizing mission-critical data. A concrete example is separating logs and backups (which might be LRS or GRS) from production databases or configuration stores that require GZRS for both zone and region protection. Document your choices and test failover behavior so the redundancy selection translates into dependable recovery.

screens.title: Azure Files and Azure Disks Use Cases
screens.narratorSegment: Azure Files and Azure Disks serve different operational roles. Azure Files provides fully managed file shares accessible via SMB, making it a natural choice for lift-and-shift applications that expect a network share or for shared configuration and media assets across VMs. For example, a legacy application that reads and writes to a network drive can be migrated with minimal changes by mounting an Azure Files share. Azure Disks provide persistent, attachable block storage for virtual machines. They behave like local hard drives attached to a VM and are the right solution when you require a boot disk, dedicated data disk, or a high-performance volume for a database running on a VM. A common misconception is assuming Azure Files can replace disks for low-latency, high-IOPS workloads; while Files has performance tiers, it does not provide the same attach and OS-disk semantics as Azure Disks. When designing your architecture, choose Azure Files for shared server files and replaceable media, and choose Disks for VM persistence and OS volumes. Also consider redundancy and performance tiers for each service and verify that your chosen option meets latency and throughput needs for production workloads.

Attachable, persistent block storage for VMs used as OS or data disks with predictable latency and IOPS.

screens.title: Azure Table and Queue Storage
screens.narratorSegment: Azure Table Storage is a lightweight NoSQL key-value store for semi-structured data. It is useful when you need simple, high-throughput storage for entities that share keys and when schema flexibility is important. Typical uses include storing device metadata, user profiles, or other wide, sparse records where relational features are unnecessary. Azure Queue Storage provides guaranteed-at-least-once delivery with simple queue semantics that decouple producers and consumers. Use queues to buffer work and smooth processing spikes between services or across microservice boundaries. A common mistake is treating Table Storage as a full document database with advanced query and transaction features; while it supports simple queries by partition and row key, it does not replace a transactional database for complex operations. For a concrete example, an ingestion pipeline can accept messages into a queue when files arrive, then workers dequeue and write metadata to Table Storage and content to Blob Storage. This separation allows each component to scale independently and simplifies retry logic. The takeaway is to use Table Storage for simple, fast key-value needs and Queue Storage to decouple processing components and handle asynchronous workloads.

screens.title: Key Concepts

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will get a practical view of the main Azure storage services and how to pick between them. We will treat storage as a set of trade-offs: object versus file versus block disk, hot versus cold access, and local versus geo redundancy. You will learn clear rules of thumb for common scenarios, such as storing data lakes, serving virtual machines, sharing files across servers, and keeping messages for asynchronous apps. I will show concrete examples, for instance when a log stream should be an append blob and when a VM operating system disk should be an Azure Disk. We will also examine access tiers and redundancy settings and why selecting the wrong one can either inflate costs or expose you to unacceptable downtime. By the end you will be able to map a workload’s access pattern, durability needs, and latency tolerance to a storage design that balances cost and reliability. Think about a scenario you manage now and imagine where those files, logs, or VM disks would live in Azure — that mental mapping will guide the lessons ahead.

These objectives focus your attention on the decisions a data engineer must make about storage. First, you will accurately differentiate the primary Azure storage services—Blob, Files, Disks, Table, and Queue—so you can pick the right technology for a workload. Second, you will identify concrete use cases for each service by matching data characteristics and access patterns to service capabilities. Third, you will explain the three core blob types—Block, Page, and Append—understand when to use each, and see examples such as data lakes, VHDs, and logging. Fourth, you will describe access tiers and how Hot, Cool, and Archive affect costs and retrieval latency, and make a sensible tier recommendation for backups versus active analytics. Each objective connects a concept to a clear design decision. Practice mapping a workload to these objectives and you will be able to justify storage choices to stakeholders.

This second objectives slide emphasizes practical application and verification. You will practice mapping a scenario to a storage plan: for example, decide whether telemetry logs belong in append blobs and which access tier suits a seven-year compliance archive. You will also practice configuring a storage account with appropriate performance and redundancy selections, and explain the cost and availability trade-offs to a stakeholder. Finally, you will evaluate when Premium block blobs are necessary for low-latency workloads versus when Standard GPv2 is sufficient. Practice scenarios include a lift-and-shift application requiring SMB file shares, a VM requiring persistent disks, a data lake using block blobs for large files, and a messaging pipeline using queues for decoupled processing. These hands-on habits make the theoretical choices concrete and defensible. Learning Objectives — Applied means translate storage features into actionable designs: pick blob type, tier, account performance, and redundancy for real workloads.. In practical terms, how you will apply these skills in practice. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Azure provides a set of storage primitives, each designed for a particular data shape and access pattern. Object storage, represented by Azure Blob Storage, holds unstructured data such as images, videos, data lake files, and backups. It is highly scalable and is the default choice when you need to store large blobs of data without a fixed schema. Azure Files is managed file storage that exposes SMB shares and is ideal when you have lift-and-shift applications that expect a network file system. Azure Disks are block-level persistent volumes attached to virtual machines; they behave like traditional hard drives and are optimized for low-latency VM workloads. For key-value or semi-structured data, Azure Table Storage offers a simple, scalable NoSQL store with high throughput. Azure Queue Storage provides simple message queuing for decoupling application components and supporting asynchronous work. A common misconception is thinking one storage type fits all workloads; in practice you must match data shape and access patterns to the most fitting primitive. For example, storing VM disks in Blob Storage is inappropriate because you need low-latency block operations and persistent attachments provided by Disks. Consider a media server storing video files: Blob Storage is the right choice. For a shared configuration folder used by multiple VMs, Azure Files is the correct fit. Always ask: what is the data shape, how often is it accessed, and what latency and transactional model does the application require?

Blob storage is the backbone for storing large amounts of unstructured data in Azure and a default choice when you need scalability and cost-efficiency. As a data engineer you will use blobs to house data lakes, raw ingestion layers, media, backups, and large export files. The key reasons are its flat namespace with containers, efficient large-object uploads, and the ability to set access tiers to manage cost according to frequency of access. A useful analogy is to think of Blob Storage as a warehouse: containers are aisles, blobs are crates. Block blobs are the standard crates used for most files; they let you upload parts in parallel for efficiency. Page blobs are like a set of indexed drawers where you can perform random reads and writes at the page granularity, and are used for virtual hard drives. Append blobs are a chronological log: each write appends to the end efficiently, making them ideal for telemetry or audit trails. A common mistake is storing append-heavy logs as block blobs and rewriting files; this causes extra operations and cost. For a concrete example, imagine ingesting sensor telemetry: use append blobs or write to a queue and flush to block blobs depending on downstream processing. The takeaway is to treat blob types as tools—choose the one that matches your read/write pattern to reduce latency and control cost.

Block blobs are designed for efficient large-file uploads. The common pattern is to split a large file into blocks, upload each block in parallel, and then commit the block list to assemble the final blob. This approach reduces end-to-end latency and improves throughput when you have large objects such as parquet files or media. A concrete example: a 10 gigabyte export can be sliced into 64 megabyte blocks, each uploaded concurrently. After all blocks are uploaded, a commit operation composes the blob from the ordered block list. Page blobs and append blobs solve two distinct problems.
